title: Guru Nanak: wonder
hookLine: the first Guru's light: wonder at the one Creator in all
tomorrow: how does a disciple become the Guru? not how you'd guess.

lines: THE SUNSET WON'T FIT ON THE SCREEN.
cards: Half the people on a beach at sunset are filming it, and the sunset never quite fits on the screen.
Simran and Maya are on the backyard trampoline after dark, phones face down for once, because Maya leaves for a different college in the fall and they're counting nights. Maya points up.
At her cousin's wedding, she says, people waved little lamps on a tray. Do Sikhs do that? Simran knows this one, sort of.
When the first Guru looked up, he saw a tray of lamps already lit. The sky was the platter.

teach.b: Tradition tells it this way. Guru Nanak came to the temple at Puri at evening worship, when lamps were waved on a platter, and he didn't join in. He sang the hymn now on Ang 13.

teach.h: SUN AND MOON ARE THE LAMPS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon are the lamps, the stars are the pearls; the scented wind is the incense, the forests are flowers. All creation is already doing the aarti.
The feeling in it has a name: vismaad, wonder.
In Asa di Var he lists it: wonder at the sound, wonder at the knowledge, wonder at the creatures, wonder at their colors. Now the debate, because Sikhs still sing this hymn, and not all the same way.
At some historic gurdwaras, lamps are waved while it's sung. Their best case: it's old custom at those seats, and the hymn about the sky is still its heart; the hands help the eyes look up.
Elsewhere, following the Sikh code, it's sung with no lamps at all. Their best case: the Guru looked away from the small tray to the big one; singing it is the aarti. Neither side stops singing it.
Here's one for a friend tonight: Guru Nanak's aarti has no lamp but the sun and the moon. Maya is quiet a while.
So wonder is the whole point, she says. Simran says: the starting point.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's aarti hymn, 'gagan mai thaal', as part of Kirtan Sohila, the prayer before sleep, and in gurdwaras in the evening; at some historic gurdwaras lamps are waved during it, while elsewhere it is sung without lamps.

o: the first Guru, whose light was wonder at all creation
the Guru who founded the city of Amritsar
a saint who wrote the Granth's closing hymns

games.q: Guru Nanak's aarti — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak's aarti hymn is sung with lamps in every gurdwara
some historic gurdwaras wave lamps; others sing it with none.
in the hymn, the stars are the pearls on the platter
Ang 13: the sky the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls.
vismaad means fear of God's power
it's wonder: at the sound, the knowledge, the creatures, their colors.

games.q: your cousin says waving lamps during the aarti hymn goes against Guru Nanak. you're asked for the other side's best case. which is it?
o: it's old custom at those seats, and the hymn about the sky stays its heart.
Guru Nanak waved lamps himself at Puri, so it's what he wanted.
the hymn isn't complete until something is actually lit.
games.why: a fair steelman keeps the shared ground: both sides sing the hymn. one keeps the old custom of lamps; one lets the sky be the only tray.

practice: Go to a window or step outside and look up for the whole sit. Find the biggest light you can see, then the smallest; in daylight, follow one cloud. Don't name anything and don't photograph it.
Just let it be bigger than you for a while.

wordCard.voice: Guru Nanak: the first Guru, whose light is wonder. He looked past the tray of lamps to the sky, and sang that it was already worshipping.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vismaad, wonder; Guru Nanak's word for awe at creation in Asa di Var.

carryVoice: For the road: wonder, the whole sky as the platter, already lit. The first of ten lights.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 13 (Raag Dhanasari, Mahalla 1, 'gagan mai thaal': the sky the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls), paraphrased
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463-464 (Asa di Var, salok Mahalla 1, 'vismaad naad vismaad ved'), paraphrased
Janamsakhi tradition: Guru Nanak at Jagannath Puri during the evening aarti
Sikh Rehat Maryada, on the singing of aarti without lamps in the gurdwara, paraphrased
